questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the common underlying pattern connecting reward hacking examples from Chapter 5 (toy environments), Chapter 6 (reward model overoptimization), Chapter 7 (RLHF failure modes), and Chapter 9 (verifier loopholes)?
options: They are unrelated problems with no shared cause

In every case, a policy optimized hard enough against a reward signal finds the gap between what that signal actually measures and what the designer truly wanted, regardless of whether the signal is a toy reward function, a learned reward model, or a rule-based verifier
They only occur when using PPO specifically, never other algorithms
They are all caused exclusively by insufficient training data
questions.explain: The lesson frames reward hacking as a recurring pattern across every type of reward signal covered in the course, not a problem unique to any one chapter or technique.

questions.q: What is the scalable oversight problem, as described in this lesson?
options: The challenge of scaling up GPU clusters for larger training runs

As models get better at tasks a human evaluator can't easily check, the human feedback that RLHF/RLAIF rest on becomes harder to trust as ground truth, since a preference label on unverifiable work is noise rather than signal
A problem that only affects image generation models, not language models
The problem of running too many parallel environments at once
questions.explain: Scalable oversight concerns supervision quality degrading as model capability on hard-to-check tasks grows, undermining the reliability of human feedback that RLHF and RLAIF depend on.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed in this lesson as an active research direction for scalable oversight?
options: Debate between models
Recursive decomposition of hard questions into checkable sub-questions
Using weaker-but-trusted models to help supervise stronger ones
Eliminating the need for any human or AI feedback entirely
questions.explain: The lesson lists debate, decomposition, and weaker-supervising-stronger as active directions — it does not claim any direction eliminates the need for feedback altogether, and explicitly states none is yet a settled answer.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say LLM-scale RL makes the sample efficiency problem more costly than it was in a Chapter 1 tabular RL setting?
options: Because tabular RL requires more rollouts than LLM-scale RL

Because every rollout in LLM-scale RL is itself a full forward pass through a billion-plus-parameter model, making a large number of needed rollouts far more expensive than in a simple tabular environment
Because LLM-scale RL never requires any rollouts at all
Because sample efficiency is not a real problem in LLM-scale RL
questions.explain: The per-rollout cost difference (a full large-model forward pass vs. a cheap tabular lookup) is what makes the same "many rollouts needed" property far more expensive at LLM scale.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about whether reward hacking, scalable oversight, and sample efficiency/generalization are fully solved problems?
options: All three have been completely solved by the techniques covered in this course
None of the three has a tidy fix; the course explicitly states that claiming otherwise would be teaching something false, and frames them as actively worked on but still open
Only reward hacking remains unsolved; the other two are fully resolved
These problems do not actually exist and were invented for this lesson
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that all three problems remain genuinely open, emphasizing honesty about the current state of the field rather than presenting a false sense of resolution.
